passages.t: Flattering lips, and words like refined silver
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. According to Sheminith. A Psalm of David” (verse 1). The prayer starts with one word: “Help, O LORD, for the godly are no more; the faithful have vanished from among men” (verse 1).

The trouble is speech. “They lie to one another; they speak with flattering lips and a double heart” (verse 2). The liars boast, “With our tongues we will prevail” (verse 4).

Then, in the middle of the psalm, God himself speaks: “For the cause of the oppressed and for the groaning of the needy, I will now arise,” says the LORD (verse 5).

The psalmist answers by setting God's words beside human words: “The words of the LORD are flawless, like silver refined in a furnace, like gold purified sevenfold” (verse 6). He trusts God to keep his people. But the last line is honest: “The wicked wander freely, and vileness is exalted among men” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
This is a lament, and Sheminith (‘the eighth’) is the same unclear musical word as in Psalm 6.

In Israel most agreements were spoken, not written. Courts, trade and promises between neighbours all rested on a person's word. So a land full of lies was a land where the weak had no protection. ‘A double heart’ is in Hebrew ‘a heart and a heart’: one heart for what you say, another for what you mean.

Verse 6 comes from the workshop. Silver ore was heated in a furnace so that the waste came away. ‘Sevenfold’ means completely, since seven is the Bible's number of completeness. Human words are full of slag. God's words have none.

Notice the shape. God's own word stands near the centre of the psalm, with human lies on both sides of it.
passages.later:
Other Scriptures use the same picture of God's word. “Every word of God is flawless; He is a shield to those who take refuge in Him” (Proverbs 30:5). David sings almost the same line in 2 Samuel 22:31 and Psalm 18:30.

Jesus asked for plain speech: “Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37). James writes that the tongue is small “but it boasts of great things” (James 3:5), the very boast of Psalm 12:4.
passages.asks:
The psalm asks you to notice how much harm words can do, and to watch your own. Is there a ‘double heart’ in how you speak, kind to someone's face and cruel behind their back?

It also gives a prayer for times when it seems no one can be trusted. Say ‘Help, O LORD.’ Then rest on the one word that has no slag in it. The psalm does not pretend the trouble is over (verse 8). It trusts anyway.
